article_title: Student understanding of Fermi energy, the Fermi-Dirac distribution and total electronic energy of a free electron gas
citation: Paul Justice, Emily Marshman, and Chandralekha Singh. (2019). Student understanding of Fermi energy, the Fermi-Dirac distribution and total electronic energy of a free electron gas. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Student+understanding+of+Fermi+energy%2C+the+Fermi-Dirac+distribution+and+total+electronic+energy%22+Justice+Marshman+Singh
title: Validated clicker question sequence (CQS) on the free electron gas integrating conceptual and quantitative knowledge
description: A sequenced set of clicker questions on the Fermi energy, density of states, total electronic energy and distribution functions, developed and validated iteratively with three physics faculty and think-aloud interviews with students. The CQS has 11 questions at T = 0 K and six at T > 0 K, and was "sequenced to balance difficulties, avoid change of both concept and context between consecutive questions as appropriate in order to avoid a cognitive overload, and include a mix of abstract and concrete questions". It was implemented with peer interaction in an upper-level undergraduate QM course after traditional lecture-based instruction.
requirements: Questions must build on each other based upon learning objectives and be interpreted unambiguously, as ensured by iteration with physics faculty and student interviews.
constraints: The article notes tutorial worksheets might have been more effective for developing procedural knowledge, but the CQS was chosen for logistical reasons since more instructors use clickers.
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics students in a junior/senior-level quantum mechanics course
graduate students after core quantum and statistical mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: calculate the Fermi energy from free electron number density and recognize it is not extensive
calculate the total electronic energy and recognize it is extensive
write, distinguish and graph the Fermi-Dirac, Bose-Einstein and Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution functions and their limiting behavior
examples: Administered in two class periods in an upper-level undergraduate QM course after traditional lecture-based instruction, with students talking to a peer before voting via clickers.
key_sources: Paul Justice, Emily Marshman, and Chandralekha Singh. (2019). Student understanding of Fermi energy, the Fermi-Dirac distribution and total electronic energy of a free electron gas. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Student+understanding+of+Fermi+energy%2C+the+Fermi-Dirac+distribution+and+total+electronic+energy%22+Justice+Marshman+Singh

article_title: Development, validation and in-class evaluation of a sequence of clicker questions on Larmor precession of spin in quantum mechanics
citation: Paul Justice, Emily Marshman, and Chandralekha Singh. (2019). Development, validation and in-class evaluation of a sequence of clicker questions on Larmor precession of spin in quantum mechanics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Development+validation+and+in-class+evaluation+of+a+sequence+of+clicker+questions+on+Larmor+precession+of+spin+in+quantum+mechanics
title: Larmor precession of spin clicker question sequence (CQS)
description: A validated sequence of six conceptual multiple-choice clicker questions (CQ1-CQ6) on the time-dependence of expectation values in the context of Larmor precession of spin, developed for "students in upper-level undergraduate QM courses taken by physics juniors and seniors". The sequence builds on the learning goals and inquiry-based guided sequences of a research-validated QuILT and on previously individually validated clicker questions. The first two questions address time development of states initially in or out of an energy eigenstate, CQ3-CQ4 address general characteristics of expectation-value time dependence, and CQ5-CQ6 contrast an Sx eigenstate with an energy eigenstate.
requirements: Questions build on each other according to the three learning goals and are worded unambiguously, refined via faculty feedback and student think-aloud interviews
Can be used separately from the QuILT or synergistically with the corresponding QuILT after the CQS
constraints: In this implementation the CQS was meant to act primarily as a "second coat" to reinforce learning after traditional lecture-based instruction
Question 5 showed persistent difficulty, suggesting room for improvement in addressing the second learning goal
target_learners: Upper-level undergraduate physics juniors and seniors in quantum mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding time-independence of expectation values of observables whose operators commute with the Hamiltonian (Ehrenfest's theorem)
Understanding that expectation values are time-independent for stationary states
Distinguishing stationary states from eigenstates of operators that do not commute with the Hamiltonian
examples: Implemented with peer discussion in two upper-level QM classes at a large research university in two consecutive years, right after the pretest in one class period
key_sources: Paul Justice, Emily Marshman, and Chandralekha Singh. (2019). Development, validation and in-class evaluation of a sequence of clicker questions on Larmor precession of spin in quantum mechanics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Development+validation+and+in-class+evaluation+of+a+sequence+of+clicker+questions+on+Larmor+precession+of+spin+in+quantum+mechanics

article_title: Development, validation and in-class evaluation of a sequence of clicker questions on Larmor precession of spin in quantum mechanics
citation: Paul Justice, Emily Marshman, and Chandralekha Singh. (2019). Development, validation and in-class evaluation of a sequence of clicker questions on Larmor precession of spin in quantum mechanics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Development+validation+and+in-class+evaluation+of+a+sequence+of+clicker+questions+on+Larmor+precession+of+spin+in+quantum+mechanics
title: Clicker question sequence design balancing difficulty, concept-context continuity, and abstract-concrete mix
description: A design pattern for sequencing clicker questions on a single concept across a few class periods, in which questions "build on each other effectively and strive to help students organize, extend and repair their knowledge structure pertaining to the topic". Questions are sequenced to balance difficulties, avoid change of both concept and context between consecutive questions to avoid cognitive overload, and mix abstract and concrete questions. The article applied this pattern in developing the six-question Larmor precession CQS from QuILT learning goals.
requirements: Sequencing validated via in-class use and faculty feedback
Prior knowledge of the topic from traditional instruction, since the CQS acts as reinforcement
constraints: Very few documented efforts exist toward systematic development and validation of clicker question sequences, per the article
target_learners: Upper-level undergraduate physics students in quantum mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: Building a coherent knowledge structure of a physics concept across a question sequence
examples: The Larmor precession CQS begins with time development of energy eigenstates (CQ1-CQ2), moves to expectation-value time dependence (CQ3-CQ4), and contrasts an Sx eigenstate with an energy eigenstate (CQ5-CQ6)

article_title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes
citation: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh (2024). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://journals.aps.org/prper
title: Balancing efficiency and innovation with peer interaction: the theoretical framework guiding CQS integration with lectures
description: The article's framework combines Schwartz et al.'s Preparation for Future Learning balance of efficiency and innovation with peer interaction under the ICAP framework. Integrating CQSs with lectures lets "the efficiency of lectures paired with the innovation of productive struggle during CQS administration and discussion" develop adaptive rather than routine experts. Under ICAP, in-person CQS discussion places students in the Interactive mode, while the online year's individual polling placed them in the Constructive mode.
requirements: CQS questions must be integrated with lectures and include opportunities for peer and whole-class discussion
Student difficulties should be used as resources to guide development and validation of the questions
constraints: In the online implementation, time constraints and technology affordances resulted in a largely absent groupwork component, so students worked in the Constructive rather than Interactive mode
target_learning_goals: two-state quantum system formalism including inner and outer products, Dirac notation, and change of basis
examples: The CQS was administered after lecture-based instruction as a content review, with clicker polling and class discussion in person and Zoom polls online
key_sources: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh (2024). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://journals.aps.org/prper

article_title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes
citation: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh (2024). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://journals.aps.org/prper
title: Clicker Question Sequence on basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems
description: A research-validated sequence of multiple-choice clicker questions for upper-level undergraduate QM courses, organized in three subsequences: CQS 1.1-1.4 on properties of two-state spin systems, CQS 2.1-2.6 on translating between Dirac notation and matrix representation and calculating inner and outer products, and CQS 3.1-3.5 on changing basis via direct substitution, projections, and spectral decomposition of unity. Questions are "carefully sequenced to build on one another" and include both concrete and abstract questions, developed iteratively from a QuILT on Dirac notation and validated through think-aloud interviews with five students.
requirements: Students complete a pre-test after traditional lecture-based instruction before engaging with the sequence
Instructor-led discussion slides between some questions to review and emphasize concepts
constraints: Designed for upper-level undergraduate QM courses and adapted from a QuILT with an eye toward condensing material under greater time constraints
target_learners: junior- and senior-level undergraduate physics students
target_learning_goals: inner and outer products
translation between Dirac notation and matrix representation
change of basis for two-state quantum systems
examples: Implemented over two to three class sessions in three consecutive years, one online via Zoom polls and two in person with clickers
key_sources: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh (2024). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with basics and change of basis for two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://journals.aps.org/prper

article_title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with time-development of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in virtual and in-person classes
citation: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh. (2021). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with time-development of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in virtual and in-person classes. https://stacks.iop.org/EJP/43/025704/mmedia
title: Research-validated clicker question sequence (CQS) on time-development of two-state quantum systems
description: A sequence of thirteen research-validated clicker questions targeting upper-level junior-/senior-level quantum mechanics students, organized into four subsections by learning goal. As the article states, "The thirteen questions in the CQS focused on the following four learning goals": identifying properties of energy eigenstates or stationary states, transforming an initial state to its time-evolved state, expressing a state in the energy eigenbasis before applying the time-evolution operator, and calculating time-dependence of expectation values. Questions were drafted, discussed and iterated to minimize unintended interpretations, standardized in terminology, and designed to avoid burdensome calculations so the sequence fits limited class time.
requirements: Administration across three lecture sessions with instructor-led discussion of answer options after each poll
A validated pre- and post-test to determine effectiveness
Checkpoints at which the instructor explains broader themes related to the previous questions
constraints: Designed for two-state systems with time-independent Hamiltonians in upper-level quantum mechanics courses
Peer Instruction was not implemented in full in the virtual 2020 setting
target_learning_goals: time-evolution of quantum states
properties of stationary states
change of basis to the energy eigenbasis
time-dependence of expectation values
examples: Implemented as a Zoom poll in fall 2020 with the instructor sharing questions on screen, and in person in fall 2021 with fully-realized Peer Instruction
key_sources: Peter Hu, Yangqiuting Li, and Chandralekha Singh. (2021). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with time-development of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in virtual and in-person classes. https://stacks.iop.org/EJP/43/025704/mmedia

article_title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes
citation: Hu, P., Li, Y., & Singh, C. (2022). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01978
title: Clicker Question Sequence (CQS) on measurement uncertainty for two-state quantum systems
description: A research-validated sequence of seventeen multiple-choice questions for upper-level undergraduate QM courses, addressing four learning goals: identifying well-defined observables, calculating measurement uncertainty and the generalized uncertainty principle, features and commutation relations of spin operators, and compatible vs. incompatible observables. The article states that "research-validated multiple-choice questions comprise an easy-to-implement instructional tool that serves to scaffold student learning and formatively assess students’ knowledge." Questions build on each other and include complex multiple-choice formats with immediate feedback and class discussion.
requirements: Implementation requires dedicating two to three consecutive 50-minute class sessions for the pre-test, CQS, and post-test
An electronic response system (clickers or Zoom polls) to track student responses in real time
constraints: Some questions involve more calculation than typical conceptual clicker questions, requiring instructors to give more time
The complex multiple-choice format may increase student cognitive load
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics students in quantum mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: identifying well-defined observables in a given quantum state
calculating measurement uncertainty and applying the generalized uncertainty principle
commutation relations of spin operators and successive measurements
compatible vs. incompatible observables
examples: Implemented via Zoom polls online and a classroom clicker system in person, with instructor-led whole-class discussion after each vote
key_sources: Hu, P., Li, Y., & Singh, C. (2022). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01978

article_title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes
citation: Hu, P., Li, Y., & Singh, C. (2022). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01978
title: Clicker question sequence design: scaffolded validated questions building on each other with whole-class discussion
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which research-validated multiple-choice questions are sequenced so that they build on each other and systematically target a coherent set of learning goals derived from common student difficulties. The article notes that "since the CQS questions build on each other, they typically take less time to complete than if the questions were not part of a sequence." After each vote the instructor displays results and leads a full class discussion, providing immediate feedback and scaffolding. The pattern was applied to measurement uncertainty in two-state quantum systems in a junior-/senior-level QM course.
requirements: Questions validated through iterative review and think-aloud interviews to minimize unintended interpretations
Coverage prioritized toward conceptual knowledge and common difficulties, avoiding burdensome calculations to fit allotted class time
A response system and instructor-led discussion after each question
constraints: The Peer Instruction small-group discussion component was largely forgone in the online administration due to difficulty adapting it
Complex multiple-choice formats may increase student cognitive load, though the authors and others have used them for parsimony across multiple facets of a concept
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics students in quantum mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: understanding measurement uncertainty, well-defined observables, and compatible vs. incompatible observables in two-state quantum systems
examples: CQS 3.4-3.5 were added for the in-person implementation after online students struggled with the eigenvalue of a measurement of S², and Q5e performance rose from 48% to 80%
key_sources: Hu, P., Li, Y., & Singh, C. (2022). Challenges in addressing student difficulties with measurement uncertainty of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.01978
